title: Is The Epstein Investigation Almost Over? Depends On Who You Ask.
author: Stephen Neukam
summary: Oversight Chair James Comer told NOTUS he expects new activity at the Justice Department as a result of his probe.
content: Republicans, led by Oversight Committee Chair James Comer (R-Kentucky), are finalizing plans to wrap up their Jeffrey Epstein investigation as the midterm elections near, with Comer indicating that the committee will probably make criminal referrals in the case. J. Scott Applewhite/AP Republicans and Democrats on the House Oversight Committee say they want the same thing: justice for the victims of the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. But whether the committee’s investigation is wrapping up or just starting will depend entirely on the November election. Republicans leading the investigation now are finishing interviews and a report as the midterm elections near, hoping to prompt the Justice Department to investigate individuals from the network surrounding Epstein. Democrats, who think they’ll control the panel in January, say there’s a lot more to mine before the probe is over. Republicans, led by Oversight Committee Chair James Comer (R-Kentucky), are finalizing plans to wrap up their Epstein investigation as the midterm elections near, with Comer indicating that the committee will probably make criminal referrals in the case. Top Justice Department officials signaled earlier this year there would be no more prosecutions after a review of millions of files related to Epstein. “The Department of Justice said the case was closed when we started it,” Comer told NOTUS about the probe into the network surrounding Epstein. He predicted a report and criminal referrals from his panel will force new action from the Justice Department, even if that work continues after his tenure. “I’m going to go out on a limb and say the case will be reopened when we’re done.” Comer, who is term-limited in his position at the top of the committee even if Republicans keep the House, has hauled a list of 19 high-profile witnesses in for closed-door interviews. Some witnesses including former President Bill Clinton and Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates told the committee they barely knew Epstein and had no knowledge of his crimes. Others, such as billionaire Leon Black , detailed a closer relationship with Epstein but issued the same denials about any illegal activity related to sexual misconduct. Among the witnesses are people with deep ties to Republican and Democratic figures. The group includes billionaire Les Wexner, a longtime Democratic donor; former Trump Attorney General Bill Barr; former Obama White House Counsel Kathy Ruemmler; and former Trump Labor Secretary Alex Acosta. Black, who has donated significantly to both parties, drew intense scrutiny from investigators in the past few months. The private equity billionaire told investigators he paid Epstein over $ million for tax and estate planning between and . That was after Epstein pleaded guilty in in Florida to soliciting prostitution from a minor. Comer issued subpoenas after Black declined to answer some of the panel's key questions during a voluntary interview in June : one subpoena for a deposition, and another for nondisclosure agreements that lawmakers maintain are between Black and women who may have been associated with Epstein. Black has turned over one NDA to investigators, a source familiar with the matter said. Investigators say they’re looking into whether any witnesses lied during their testimony. According to Comer, victims have said some of the people deposed have made untrue statements. “We’re doing everything in our ability, and we’re going to continue to work with the victims,” Comer said. Democrats have criticized Republicans’ handling of the Epstein probe, pointing out that witnesses were not required to testify under oath and that Comer did not publicly release recordings of most of the interviews (save for Bill and Hillary Clinton). California Rep. Robert Garcia, currently the top Democrat on the oversight panel, is in line to take over if his party wins the House and says the investigation has a lot more ground to cover. “There’s no question that the investigation will continue into the next couple of years,” Garcia told NOTUS. “The fact that the chairman has been unwilling to put most of the interviews under oath is really problematic, and there’s a lot of folks who are still going to have more information.” But Randall Eliason, a former assistant U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, told NOTUS that the fight over whether to swear in witnesses is mostly about “atmospherics” and that “legally, it doesn’t matter.” “Whether or not you are under oath, lying to Congress during an investigation is a crime,” Eliason said. “It certainly wouldn’t prevent someone from bringing criminal charges if they thought the elements were there.” Despite their criticisms of Comer’s probe, Democrats told NOTUS they would support criminal referrals stemming from the investigation. “I’d want to wait and see who exactly Chairman Comer is considering, but we would be supportive of going after folks,” Garcia told NOTUS. “We think there’s enough evidence for the Justice Department to take stronger action.” California Rep. Ro Khanna, another Democrat on the panel who teamed up with Kentucky GOP Rep. Thomas Massie to force the release of the files, told NOTUS he supports criminal referrals. “We need a call to remove people with serious allegations from their positions on important corporations or boards, or having their names on important buildings,” Khanna said. “And we need a clear call for the release of the rest of the files.” The Justice Department released about 3.5 million pages of documents related to the Epstein investigation after a veto-proof majority of Congress passed a bill forcing the federal government to publicly turn them over. Batches of the files were released late last year, featuring heavy redactions and the accidental release of sensitive information related to victims. The Justice Department withheld more than 2 million pages, citing the privacy of victims, privileged information and other legally protected content. Comer is still planning to bring in several additional witnesses before concluding the investigation this fall. Black is scheduled to return for another interview with the committee on Sept. 3. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, who could be confirmed by the Senate to permanently take the top post at Justice soon, is supposed to speak with the panel after that process concludes. Blanche, who at the time was the no. 2 official at the DOJ, oversaw the release of the Epstein files, according to former Attorney General Pam Bondi. The White House and Blanche are under public pressure to show they are responding to questions about Epstein’s misconduct and the unreleased Epstein files. President Donald Trump ran in vowing to bring those involved in illegal actions to justice, but last summer began dismissing the political controversy surrounding the files as a “hoax” conjured by political foes. Blanche questions about his handling of the Epstein investigation during his Senate confirmation process. He told the committee there are “no closed investigations” in regard to Epstein’s crimes. “If we learn today, if we learn next week, if we learn next month that there’s an individual we can investigate, indict and prosecute out of the Epstein files, you better believe that we will,” Blanche said at his confirmation hearing in July. This summer, Comer told NOTUS he wanted to hold public hearings with some of Epstein’s victims, and signaled that he is working closely with victims as he moves to conclude the probe. It would be the first public hearing on the Epstein investigation. Wrapping up the investigation means Comer must navigate the rocky internal politics inside his own party. Vice President JD Vance recently criticized the administration’s handling of the files in a podcast interview, a sentiment Comer echoed. But the congressman, like the vice president, has also downplayed Trump’s connection to Epstein, sharing the president’s argument that Democrats are engaged in a political witchhunt: “All [Democrats] care about on Epstein is Trump,” Comer told NOTUS. Massie pointed to Vance’s comments as proof of the delicate balance some Republicans are trying to strike. “[Vance is] at the same time trying to put daylight between himself and the debacle of the Epstein files that’s been committed by this administration, and also try to ameliorate the damage that’s been done there,” Massie told NOTUS. For Democrats waiting in the wings to take over the investigation, there is a massive hole in the probe that they want to fill in. “Quite frankly, there’s a lot of unanswered questions about the president,” Garcia said. “Until we get those 3 million documents released by the DOJ, this investigation is not going to be over.”

title: Senate Confirms Erica Schwartz to Lead the CDC
author: Margaret Manto
summary: Schwartz served as deputy surgeon general during Trump’s first administration.
content: Erica Schwartz will be the CDC’s first permanent director in nearly a year. Mariam Zuhaib/AP Erica Schwartz, who was the deputy U.S. surgeon general during the first Trump administration, will serve as the director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The Senate confirmed her nomination Wednesday. When sworn in, Schwartz will be the CDC’s first permanent director in nearly a year, taking over an agency that’s been at the center of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s attempts to transform the nation’s vaccine policies. The last permanent director, Susan Monarez, was ousted from the role last August after disagreeing with Kennedy on vaccine policies. National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya has led the CDC in an acting capacity since Monarez’s departure. The CDC has been rocked by a series of challenges over the past two years, including the measles and hantavirus outbreaks , personnel and funding cuts , and a shooting at its Atlanta campus last summer that killed one police officer. The agency has also been targeted by the administration with efforts to roll back its vaccine policy, efforts that drew the ire of Sen. Bill Cassidy, who chairs the Senate Committee for Health, Education, Labor and Pensions. Cassidy ultimately said he would support Schwartz after the CDC updated a website about vaccines and autism to remove a reference to him. Schwartz, the former chief medical officer of the Coast Guard, told Cassidy during her confirmation hearing that she would “never betray the science.”

title: Todd Blanche's Nomination Is in Jeopardy After Sen. Collins Says She'll Vote No
author: Al Weaver
summary: The acting attorney general needs to secure one more vote from either of two Republican holdouts: Cassidy or Murkowski.
content: Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche still needs to secure support from another Senate Republican to win confirmation to permanently lead the Justice Department. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche has moved to within a single vote of winning confirmation to lead the Justice Department, but his path narrowed after Maine Sen. Susan Collins, one of three remaining Republican holdouts, announced Tuesday evening she will vote against his nomination as it finally heads toward the Senate floor. “While I believe Mr. Blanche is a capable lawyer, the Department of Justice has become increasingly political. Mr. Blanche has taken several actions that have further eroded the Department’s independence, and that is the basis for my vote to oppose his confirmation,” Collins said in a statement. After weeks of intense talks, the acting attorney general finally cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday morning, having struck a deal over the weekend with Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) to nix a controversial “anti-weaponization fund” and limit the scope of President Donald Trump’s audit immunity deal with the IRS. However, he got a mixed bag of results after that committee vote. Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) handed him a boost by announcing he would support Blanche on the floor. Hours later, though, Collins revealed that she will oppose him. This puts Blanche on a tightrope, as he must win over at least one of the two remaining holdouts to be confirmed. Collins nodded at Blanche’s initial decision to green-light a settlement with Trump that created the $1.8 billion Justice Department fund, which drew significant derision among Senate Republicans, and the immunity deal that would have shielded Trump from future IRS audit scrutiny , as key reasons for her decision. However, she went even further, pointing to Blanche’s reported plan to roll back abortion access and the DOJ’s attempt to indict Sens. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan) over “their ill-advised, but constitutionally protected, videos” encouraging military members to resist unlawful orders. “For these reasons, I will vote against this nomination,” she said. Before Curtis gave his support Tuesday, he had indicated that his decision hinged on the deal secured by Cornyn and Tillis. He met with Blanche last week. “I’ve been pleased with his receptivity and understanding of the issues raised by my colleagues and me, including the anti-weaponization fund and a number of Utah-specific priorities,” he said in a social media post. “I look forward to working with him once confirmed.” With Collins and Curtis going public, that leaves two outstanding Senate Republicans who are undecided: Alaska Sen. Lisa Murkowski and Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy. Murkowski, a preeminent centrist vote, told reporters that she is “going to have to have a few more conversations” with Blanche, but called the order killing the “anti-weaponization” fund a “pretty good step” on Monday. “I’m going to find out more. I’d like to find out a little bit more about the negotiations over the weekend and I haven’t had a chance to do that,” she said, conceding that it “says a lot” that the pair of Judiciary Committee members made the deal. Cassidy declined to comment repeatedly when pressed about Blanche. Blanche and Republicans can lose no more than two votes on the floor due to Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-Kentucky) ongoing absence , assuming there is full attendance otherwise. The timing of a floor vote is also unclear. Senate GOP leaders have an ambitious agenda to complete before the chamber breaks for the five-week recess. Senate leaders are trying to get unanimous consent to expedite passage of a stopgap spending bill through mid-December and the Russia sanctions package that won massive bipartisan support in an initial vote last week. They are also attempting to get the ball rolling on a cryptocurrency regulation bill and legislation protecting college athletes before departing town. However, Blanche appears to be a priority. One Senate GOP aide, who requested anonymity to discuss private leadership plans, said there is a high likelihood that Blanche’s confirmation gets completed — which could keep the chamber in session into the weekend. Tuesday’s committee vote took place only days after Chair Chuck Grassley was forced to cancel a vote late last week. Cornyn and Tillis finally struck a deal with Blanche and the Justice Department late Sunday, with both members emphasizing that it was not simply made for their benefit, as others in the Senate Republican conference have been worried about the proposed fund. “Their concerns about the anti-weaponization fund and the IRS settlement were shared by many, including this senator,” Grassley said during Tuesday’s markup. “I am grateful that they, as well as Mr. Blanche and the White House, worked in good faith to resolve them. Formally rescinding the anti-weaponization fund and clarifying the scope of the release of claims has put this issue to bed once and for all." Beyond Curtis, Blanche has picked up other key votes in recent days. Sens. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), a pair of incumbents who are up for reelection in November, both signaled that they plan to support him. Husted told Punchbowl News that he is a “yes” vote pending a read-through of the deal struck with Cornyn and Tillis. Sullivan noted that Blanche traveled to Alaska in recent weeks in an effort to “understand our state, understand the challenges either before or after your confirmation, and he did that.” “He’s committed to working on a bunch of issues that really matter to Alaska,” Sullivan told NOTUS. “So I’m supportive.”

title: Rand Paul’s Fauci Diary Dump Exposed Peoples’ Medical Histories
author: Margaret Manto
summary: The Republican senator’s office published over 20 individuals’ health information without redaction.
content: Sen. Rand Paul published over 1, pages of Fauci’s diaries last week ahead of Anthony Fauci’s appearance before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP Anthony Fauci’s diary included the names and medical information of people he came into contact with as director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, including people with cancer, Ebola or HIV. Sen. Rand Paul’s office published Fauci’s diary entries without redacting those sensitive details. The documents expose more than 20 individuals by name along with their medical histories, a NOTUS review found. Paul published over 1, pages of Fauci’s diaries last week ahead of Fauci’s appearance before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, after obtaining the documents from the Department of Health and Human Services. The initial document dump was unredacted. Days later, those files were removed and replaced with partial redactions to some, but not all, of the personal medical information. The unredacted entries have raised legal questions around how the Health Department disclosed these documents to the Senate. Several of the individuals named in the documents said they were unaware their medical history had been made public and expressed concerns around their personal privacy. “What this administration does with information is selective, it is unconstitutional and truly disappointing,” Leslie Adelman, one of the individuals whose medical information was revealed in the documents, told NOTUS in a text message. Adelman said she was “pretty offended that my name and public health information have been shared to the world.” NOTUS is only publishing the names of the private individuals who have given direct approval to appear in this story. Fauci’s diary entries remain accessible with some redactions on Paul’s Senate office website. Paul, who has long called for Fauci to be jailed for his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic, has suggested that the documents reveal that Fauci thought the COVID-19 virus emerged from a lab. The senator continues to promote the documents on social media. HHS provided the documents to Paul in response to an oversight request, not a subpoena, an agency spokesperson, Grace Davis Jamison, said in a statement provided to NOTUS. In an interview with Fox News, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said HHS provided the documents to Paul’s office after his team uncovered them on government servers. The published records include names, diagnoses, symptoms and test results of individuals. Two of the people identified by name alongside their medical details were children, including the child of Trump administration staffer Stephen Miller and his wife, Katie Miller. Katie Miller previously told NOTUS that Paul’s office published the details of her child’s medical care without her knowledge or permission. They were subsequently redacted. Some of the named individuals are public figures, including President Donald Trump and former President Joe Biden. Others appear to be private individuals whose medical history has never been publicly released before. One Ebola patient’s medical saga is recounted in detail across over 30 pages. Paul’s office did not respond to a request for comment. There is no indication that Fauci intended for the unredacted notes to become public. Some of the entries that included medical information were labeled by Fauci as “confidential.” In his opening statement before the Senate committee, Fauci said that Paul’s release of his “unredacted personal diary” was intended to embarrass and intimidate him, and accused the senator of having an “unhinged obsession” with jailing him. Fauci repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment during the hearing. Fauci did not respond to a request for comment. A person close to Fauci said in a text message that Fauci “never intended for any of his personal diary entries to be made public. They were his own personal notes/reflections to himself.” In a series of posts on X , Paul called the released documents a “personal account of building the federal biodefense complex” and wrote that they reveal the former health official’s “love for the newfound fame COVID brought him.” The documents include Fauci’s recounting of patients he met in passing who seemingly have nothing to do with either biodefense or COVID. In an entry dated to Oct. 26, , he wrote of visiting Adelman, a patient at the National Institutes of Health Clinical Center, at her request. “Went to Clinical Center to visit a young woman (Leslie Adelman) who has Von Hipple-Lindau disease and had a hemangioblastoma in her cerebellum removed last week,” Fauci wrote. “Since she was in the hospital she asked her neurosurgeon Dr. Kareem Zaghloul if it were possible to meet me. I, of course, said yes and went to see her. Quite a time. Nurses and physicians all wanted pictures with me. Leslie was delighted. Made my day.” Adelman confirmed Fauci’s account of their meeting. “He made my day even more,” she told NOTUS. She also expressed frustration at what she viewed as the federal government’s differing standards for releasing personal information. “If I was a victimizer in the Epstein files, my name would have been redacted,” Adelman said. “Instead, I am an innocent and productive member of society, who has donated her time and body to NIH for research that will benefit millions of people — yet MY name and information is blasted to the national news.” The released documents also include extensive detail on American medical providers who contracted Ebola during the - outbreak, and whose care Fauci was closely involved with. Craig Spencer, an emergency room physician who contracted Ebola and whose medical information was included in the released documents, called it “stupid and irresponsible” that they were published. “My information out there doesn’t do anything or highlight anything,” Spencer said. Spencer’s name and information was redacted in the updated versions of the released documents. Adelman’s medical information was not. Of two HIV-positive individuals that Fauci recounted meeting in the early 2000s, one name was redacted, but not the other. This is not the first time the Trump administration has released files without redacting personal information. Last year, it released thousands of pages related — some only barely — to the assassination of John F. Kennedy. Those pages also contained the personal information, including Social Security numbers, of hundreds of congressional staff members, intelligence researchers and an ambassador. The White House later acknowledged that it only began looking through the JFK files for personal information after they were already published. It directed the Social Security Administration to issue new numbers to the people who were affected, as well as offer them free credit monitoring. Earlier this year, the Justice Department withdrew several thousand documents it published related to Jeffrey Epstein after it was found that they contained unredacted information and media pertaining to Epstein’s victims, including nude photos, names and email addresses. A federal judge is also currently reviewing whether the Justice Department over-redacted documents tied to Epstein it released under the Epstein Files Transparency Act. The fact that the Fauci documents were released by HHS voluntarily and not under a subpoena may mean the individuals named in them have a constitutional claim against the agency, one privacy expert said — though another said it would be exceedingly difficult. “The Fifth Amendment and the 14th Amendment have been read by a number of federal circuit courts to provide a right of informational privacy, which protects against situations like this,” said John Davisson, deputy director and director of enforcement at the Electronic Privacy Information Center. “The disclosure of sensitive personal information, health information, is often implicated in claims like this without a corresponding legitimate basis for disclosure.” He , “It’s hard to imagine that this kind of bulk disclosure of sensitive health information serves any sort of legitimate, compelling government interest.” It would be very difficult, if not impossible, for any of the impacted individuals to assert a constitutional claim in this circumstance due to the “distorted path” the documents took to publication, said Sharona Hoffman, a professor of law and bioethics at Case Western Reserve University. “This doesn’t fit squarely into any of the privacy laws,” Hoffman said. “It’s just sort of bizarre behavior.” When contacted by NOTUS, individuals whose medical information was published in the documents said they were frustrated both by the release of their information and by the continued criticism of Fauci. “All I will say is this man does not deserve any of this SHIT that he and his family are going through,” Carla Heeke Dean, a former patient of Fauci’s whose medical information was included in the documents, said in an email.

title: Blanche Clears Crucial Committee Vote With Confirmation Still on Thin Ice
author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
summary: Several Republicans in the narrowly divided Senate have not publicly confirmed they will back him.
content: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein The Senate Judiciary Committee voted Tuesday to advance Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general after two Republican holdouts ended their opposition. Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) had called for Blanche to submit an order in writing killing President Donald Trump’s now-rescinded $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund, as well as a separate order placing limits on a legal settlement that shielded the president and his businesses from IRS audits. After weeks of back-and-forth, Blanche penned two one-page documents over the weekend that purported to fulfill Cornyn and Tillis’ demands, ending the impasse. “I’m going to support Mr. Blanche’s nomination, but what I hope I see out of him is a bending of the curve of this absurdity,” Tillis said shortly before the committee voted, describing what he characterized as “weaponization” of the Justice Department by both parties. Blanche’s nomination now heads to a full Senate vote, though several Republicans have not publicly confirmed they will back him. Blanche can only afford to lose two Republican votes, assuming that all 47 members of the Senate Democratic caucus vote no and Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky) remains absent due to health concerns. A spokesperson for Sen. Susan Collins (R–Maine) on Monday said she was undecided until she reviewed the agreement that Blanche struck with Cornyn and Tillis. Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana) have also not committed to voting in favor of Blanche’s nomination. Law experts scrutinized the documents , which appear to leave loopholes that the Trump administration could use to revive the anti-weaponization fund. Experts who spoke with NOTUS this week also cautioned that the agreement’s language left the audit immunity deal largely intact and raised questions about enforceability because it was not signed by Trump or other parties involved in litigation. Blanche could also likely undo the agreement if he is confirmed as attorney general because his order is a Justice Department document, not a court filing. Sen. Dick Durbin (D–Illinois), ranking member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, said on Tuesday that the plaintiffs involved in the Trump-IRS settlement could sue to enforce the deal. Durbin also accused Blanche of perjury, contending that Blanche stated in a private meeting with the senator that it was a “mistake” to create the fund only to walk down those words during his confirmation hearing.

title: YOLOver
author: Evan McMorris-Santoro, Jasmine Wright, Manuela Silva
content: Sen. Thom Tillis talking with reporters at the Capitol. Allison Robbert/AP Today’s notice: What did we learn from the Todd Blanche saga? What to watch for in Michigan tonight. Trump gives Iran another one last chance. And: A deep dive into how politicians make money investing donor money. THE LATEST YOLO no mo’. Did we all overhype the vision of a swashbuckling crew of wronged Republican senators out for revenge against Donald Trump ? Sens. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) and John Cornyn (R-Texas) finally agreed to advance acting Attorney General Todd Blanche ’s nomination for the permanent job on the wings of what NOTUS’ Derek Hawkins reports is an all-but-toothless promise to unwind the $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization fund” deal Trump struck with the DOJ. It was less YOLO and more YOFET (You Only Fold Every Time). That comes after Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana), the chair of the Senate health committee Trump eagerly bumped from reelection, voted last week to advance the president’s nominees to run the CDC and HHS’s disaster and public-health-crisis response office despite expressing strong reservations about both. Like Tillis and Cornyn, Cassidy eventually said he trusted the nominees to do the right thing, and voted for them. “You can’t have perfection,” he said . The key difference between how these senators treated controversial nominees before Trump squashed their careers and after is tone. The president got his nominees past the senators with some light grumbling before, and stronger grumbling after. But he got them through. “I think we did the best we could,” Cornyn told NOTUS’ Igor Bobic when asked about the deal he cut with Blanche to earn his support. But not everyone seems to agree. NOTUS’ Al Weaver reports that a couple of Republicans who have voted against controversial Trump 2.0 nominees before — Sens. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Susan Collins of Maine — said they were still not totally ready to sign on to the Blanche confirmation vote. But there are also signs they might not stand in the way for long, either. Murkowski called the deal Tillis and Cornyn cut a “pretty good step.” Open tabs: The Midterms: Primary Turnout Trends as of July (Bipartisan Policy Center); A federal judge lets DHS proceed with a border wall through a small Texas town’s levee system (AP); Author of Democrats’ Autopsy Releases ‘Missing’ Chapter (NOTUS); Manufacturing survey shows inflation worries ‘worse than pandemic era,’ adding to Fed pressure (CNBC) From Michigan Sound smart watching the Michigan Democratic Senate primary tonight. The thing to keep an eye on, from NOTUS’ Alex Roarty: turnout. One independent analysis of tonight’s vote, shared with Alex, predicted 1.6 million people would vote in the primary. If the number trends higher, that portends well for progressive Abdul El-Sayed , who polls best with people who don’t regularly vote. If fewer people turn out, however, that’s good news for establishment candidate Haley Stevens . B-plot to watch: The 13th Congressional District, which includes a sizable chunk of Detroit and some of its suburbs. Rep. Shri Thanedar is the incumbent Democrat, and party-aligned groups that have wanted to dislodge him for some time now think they have the person to do it in democratic socialist state lawmaker Donavan McKinney . NOTUS’ Christa Dutton explores a side of this race that doesn’t get as much attention: the personality part. Many people in Washington see Thanedar as kind of an odd guy, and have not rallied to his cause like they have other Democrats under pressure from the left. Thanedar will tell you this is a real thing, but also shrugs it off. “It’s not like a high school,” he told Christa. “I’m not trying to be the most popular member of Congress.” From South Carolina The new Sen. Graham out-MAGAs the last one. That was the main takeaway from last night’s South Carolina Republican Senate primary debate, where Sen. Darline Graham four candidates hoping to take the seat she was appointed to after her brother passed. Graham mentioned Trump had endorsed her in her opening remarks, and proceeded to make it impossible for any candidate on stage to be closer to the president than she was. “I am all for getting rid of the filibuster — this is where I differ from my brother — because eventually the Democrats are going to get rid of it anyway,” Graham said during a conversation about the SAVE America Act. The only candidate offering any kind of alternative was Mark Sanford , the former governor and congressman. He offered the lone MAGA-skeptical commentary on stage, dinging the president on spending and the war in Iran, but said he also supports the SAVE Act and pointed out he voted with Trump “90% of the time” when he was in Congress. From the White House Yet another last chance for Iran. From an Oval Office Q&A yesterday: Reporter : Mr. President, this is at least the fifth time you’ve called off airstrikes against Iran since April to negotiate. What is your message to the American people who are wondering what has changed this time? Why should it be any different? Trump : Well, you don’t know. I don’t know. I think we’re maybe going to get something, but I want to give them every last chance before decapitation. NOTUS PERSPECTIVES With Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis agreeing to support Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general, Matt K. Lewis asks: What is wrong with Republicans? title: Two Senators Are Convinced Trump’s IRS Deal Is Dead. Others, Not So Much.
author: Derek Hawkins
summary: Todd Blanche’s late-night documents eased political concerns, but not legal questions, on the anti-weaponization fund and immunity deal.
content: Todd Blanche’s order is not signed by President Donald Trump or other parties in that underlying litigation, raising doubt about its enforceability, experts said. Two Republican holdouts on Todd Blanche’s attorney general nomination said they got the written assurance they needed that President Donald Trump’s $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund is . But the two pages of text on Justice Department letterhead appear to carry little legal weight, according to legal experts. The documents released late Sunday by Blanche, the acting attorney general, leave ample room for the Trump administration to use other avenues to compensate the president’s allies who claim they were unfairly targeted by federal authorities. They also keep largely intact a tax-audit immunity deal for Trump and his family, which, along with the fund, was created to settle a lawsuit Trump brought against the IRS over their leaked tax returns. Blanche’s order is not signed by Trump or other parties in that underlying litigation, raising doubt about its enforceability, according to experts. And because it’s a Justice Department document, not a court filing, Blanche could undo it with the stroke of a pen if he gets the permanent job. All told, said Rupa Bhattacharyya, a former Justice Department attorney who managed victim compensation funds for the department, the order “feels like a very political move to get the nomination advanced.” “It’s not clear to me what authority or legal effect the acting attorney general has to modify the settlement agreement on his own behalf,” Bhattacharyya said. “And there’s nothing that stops him from getting confirmed and then rescinding the order that rescinded the order.” Lawyers in a federal lawsuit challenging the fund were not convinced, either. In a letter Monday to the Justice Department, they called on officials to back up Blanche’s assertions in court. They asked the government to tell them by 5 p.m. whether the Justice Department will file a written declaration saying under penalty of perjury that the fund would not proceed. “The Trump-Vance administration cannot ask the public or our clients to accept a late-night social media post in place of legally binding action,” said Skye Perryman, who heads Democracy Forward, the legal advocacy group representing the plaintiffs. Even a Trump ally and prominent backer of the anti-weaponization fund, Mike Howell of the conservative Oversight Project, acknowledged on social media how easily Blanche could reverse his order. “Can be undone after Tuesday,” Howell wrote over Blanche’s post of the document. “The Anti-Weaponization Fund is great.” Blanche published the order in an 11 p.m. social media post, calling it the product of “good faith discussions” with lawmakers who were concerned about the settlement in Trump’s IRS lawsuit. Some lawmakers had objected to the possibility that the anti-weaponization fund could be used to pay rioters from the Jan. 6, , attack on the Capitol. And they also questioned whether the immunity deal could apply to future tax issues or benefit Trump associates not named in the case. Republican Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, both on the Senate Judiciary Committee, threatened to block Blanche’s nomination without written assurance that the fund had been terminated and the deal modified. In statements Monday , the senators said they were “pleased” with what they called the “binding” order from Blanche. They are expected to vote along with other Republicans to advance his nomination out of the Judiciary Committee on Tuesday morning. The order says a May 18 directive from Blanche establishing the fund “is rescinded and shall have no force or effect.” “No Members were appointed; no funds were transferred; no process for receiving claims was established; no claims were paid,” the document states. “This order establishes, beyond any doubt, that there is no Fund.” The order also purports to limit Trump’s immunity deal, saying that it “applies by its terms only retroactively,” meaning it would not extend to people outside the lawsuit nor protect the president, his sons or their business from possible future audits. Legal experts and several Democratic lawmakers said the immunity agreement may have still wiped out tens of millions of dollars or more in potential tax liabilities from Trump and his family. “Lipstick on this rancid grift is no excuse to confirm him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut) said of Blanche. Experts also noted that the Justice Department could still pay out claims to Jan. 6 defendants and others alleging political prosecution under the Federal Tort Claims Act. “If what the senators are concerned about is that payments are going to be made to Jan. 6 defendants, the fact is, a very large number of them have filed claims under the Federal Tort Claims Act. And the Justice Department could be paying out those claims,” said Bhattacharyya, who is legal director at the Institute for Constitutional Advocacy and Protection at Georgetown Law. “The administration never needed the anti-weaponization fund to settle these claims.” Just last week, the Justice Department agreed to pay a seven-figure settlement to an anti-abortion activist, Paul Vaughn, who was convicted during the Biden administration of blocking access to an abortion clinic. Trump pardoned Vaughn while his case was on appeal. Speaking with reporters Monday, Trump defended the tax deal and anti-weaponization fund, claiming he and others were wrongfully investigated and prosecuted by previous presidential administrations. "I view that fund as a positive, and a lot of Republicans do too," Trump said. "I think Todd Blanche agreed to reconfirm things that he's already said, and what he said was OK." A Justice Department spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Barbara McQuade, a former longtime federal prosecutor, said Vaughn’s settlement “shows that they’re not done giving payouts to Trump supporters who claimed to have been the victims of weaponization.” “They’re just going to do it individually instead of through the settlement fund,” she said. “As a result, this representation by Blanche isn’t worth the paper it’s written on.”

title: Golf the Blues Away
author: Brett Bachman
content: A general view of a sign for Trump National Golf Club Bedminster on October 31, , outside Trump National Golf Club in Bedminster, NJ. Erica Denhoff/Icon Sportswire/AP Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for August 3, . You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free! THE LATEST President Donald Trump complained this morning about the “unbelievably duplicitous” Iranian regime after it denied his assertion that another round of ceasefire negotiations were set to begin. But he’s having a better time on the links. Trump, 80, apparently won the club championship at his Bedminster golf club in New Jersey over the weekend. He posted video this morning of what he called “the winning shot,” a short chip that landed within a few feet of the hole. “It’s called TALENT, and I have it, and they don’t!” Trump wrote. The House Ethics Committee recommended Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-North Carolina) for censure over what it classified as inappropriate relationships with staffers. This is the first time the committee has resorted to censure since it knocked former Rep. Charles Rangel (D-New York) in over improper fundraising, financial disclosures and failure to pay taxes. THE HILL Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) have agreed to back Trump’s attorney general nominee, Todd Blanche , after he officially agreed in writing to kill the “anti-weaponization” fund and limit a legal settlement shielding the president and his businesses from IRS audits. The Senate version of a continuing resolution released over the weekend would prohibit the Office of Management and Budget from implementing an overhaul of the federal grant-approval process that would have handed more power over to the White House. The upper chamber is scheduled to vote this evening on the short-term government funding bill. THE ADMINISTRATION The president is weighing whether to fire Jeanine Pirro over her decision to drop charges against a formern Olympian who had been accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, CNN reported . “Frankly, I think she choked, because the judge was really vicious,” Trump told reporters this afternoon. When asked whether he was reconsidering Pirro’s role, Trump called the reporter “fake news.” Embattled FIFA boss Gianni Infantino called up Marco Rubio this morning in an attempt to shore up U.S. support and protect his job. He’s facing pressure to resign after abandoning a scheme to sell off shares of the World Cup to Joshua Kushner ’s private equity firm, the New York Post reported . The U.S. dollar is weakening against the Japanese yen today after the U.S. Treasury Department made a rare intervention to prop up the floundering currency last week. The National Park Service assessed that Trump’s massive arch would “adversely” affect dozens of iconic D.C. monuments. THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL The author of the DNC’s election “autopsy” claimsrevealed that the document made public by embattled chair Ken Martin earlier this year had a missing chapter. It focused on both President Joe Biden’s ill-fated decision to run for reelection and the reasons Democratic operatives did not properly weigh voters’ affordability concerns, according to The New York Times . “That is false,” Martin told the Times. “This alleged report section was not in any binder I reviewed … If we had this in May, we would have released it with the rest of the report.” THE KING OF SHOCK AND TROLL THANK YOU FOR READING Today’s newsletter was produced by Kelly Poe and Jonann Brady. If you like it, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please subscribe — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at finalnotus@notus.com .

title: Blanche Cuts a Deal With Cornyn to Get His Nomination Back on Track
author: Al Weaver
summary: The agreement came together despite apparent opposition from Trump, who has vocally expressed support for the $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund.
content: Mariam Zuhaib/AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib Sen. John Cornyn has struck a deal with acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and the Justice Department on an in-writing order nixing the “anti-weaponization fund” and limiting the scope of the audit immunity deal struck with President Donald Trump, putting Blanche a step closer to being confirmed as attorney general. Late on Sunday, Cornyn and Blanche announced the agreement, which featured a formal order that the Texas senator and Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) had been seeking for weeks in order to advance his nomination. “Sen. Cornyn has reached an agreement with the Department of Justice,” Natalie Yezbick, a Cornyn spokeswoman, said in a statement. “[The DOJ] will be issuing a formal order permanently terminating the anti-weaponization fund and making clear in a binding written document that the scope of the audit settlement is limited to only the plaintiffs, including the President, and the IRS.” The decision comes ahead of Tuesday’s planned Senate Judiciary Committee markup, which Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Republican leaders scheduled over the weekend in the hopes that a deal would be struck. A single “no” vote from Cornyn or Tillis would have sunk Blanche’s nomination. The agreement came together despite apparent opposition from Trump, who has vocally expressed support for the $1.8 billion fund. The president late last week indicated that he was willing to temporarily withdraw Blanche’s nomination until early next year when Cornyn and Tillis, who both lost primaries this year, are set to leave office. Trump wrote on Truth Social Saturday that he was prepared to “push hard” for the fund to be codified into law despite the reservations of numerous Senate Republicans beyond Cornyn and Tillis. Blanche posted the pair of orders on his X . “My team and I have met with committee members and Senators over the past several weeks and addressed any concerns or outstanding questions,” Blanche posted shortly before Cornyn publicly agreed to the deal. “We have enjoyed good faith discussions, and as a result issue the following order and update with regard to the May IRS settlement. The Department always welcomes and appreciates productive engagement with all members of Congress.”

title: Trump Sticks by ‘Anti-Weaponization’ Fund Ahead of Blanche Confirmation Vote
author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
summary: The president stood by his controversial fund despite its jeopardization of an upcoming Senate vote for AG nominee Todd Blanche.
content: “It will immediately be back on the table,” Trump said of the fund, “and I will get it done.” Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP President Donald Trump indicated Saturday he would not waver on the controversial “anti-weaponization” fund that has threatened Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general. Trump said on Truth Social he would “push hard” to get congressional approval for the $1.8 billion pool of money — a fund that Blanche signed off on as part of the president’s settlement against the IRS. That approval would be nearly impossible to attain in the current environment: Critics from both sides of the aisle have raised concerns about offering payouts to people who participated in the Jan. 6 Capitol riots and other Trump allies. Chief among the dissenters are outgoing Sens. John Cornyn (R–Texas) and Thom Tillis (R–North Carolina), who have withheld voting for Blanche until they have receive written guarantees that the Justice Department will kill the fund. Trump accused the duo of retaliating after the president refused to back their reelection campaigns earlier this year. “It will immediately be back on the table,” Trump said of the fund, “and I will get it done.” Trump, his two eldest sons and the Trump Organization appealed the ruling on Friday to the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in hopes of blocking the ruling a federal judge made earlier this month that Trump and the Justice Department had manipulated the judicial process to benefit the president and his allies. Trump repeated on Saturday he was willing to leave Blanche as acting attorney general until Cornyn and Tillis are out of office next year. Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley (R–Iowa) rescheduled a vote for Blanche on Tuesday, but Cornyn and Tillis have signaled they will not change their positions. “President Trump clearly intends to resurrect the payout pot for punks either by inappropriately establishing another bogus fund or pushing Congress to vote for a bill that the majority of Republicans in the Senate would be against,” Tillis wrote on Saturday in response to Trump. “It’s unfortunate that Todd Blanche, who I consider qualified for the job, will not be confirmed because of this reversal.”

title: Trump Files Appeal to Reinstate His ‘Anti-Weaponization’ Fund
author: Torrie Herrington
summary: Critics are concerned the pool of money will be used to pay settlements to people who participated in the Jan. 6 Capitol riots and other allies of the president.
content: President Donald Trump's "anti-weaponization" fund has drawn bipartisan criticism in Congress and stalled the confirmation process for acting Attorney General Todd Blanche. Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo President Donald Trump filed an appeal Friday in hopes of reinstating his controversial “anti-weaponization” fund, which has drawn criticism from lawmakers in both parties and derailed the confirmation process for his attorney general pick, Todd Blanche. The president, his two eldest sons and the Trump Organization filed the notice of appeal in the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, based in Atlanta, to review the decision a federal judge made earlier this month that ruled Trump and the Justice Department had manipulated the judicial process to benefit the president and his allies. Critics are concerned the pool of money will be used to pay settlements to people who participated in the Jan. 6 Capitol riots and other allies of the president. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche has declined to follow the judge’s orders to put in writing that the fund had been killed, instead saying his previous public verbal assurances that the agency would not issue payouts should be sufficient. Blanche’s Senate confirmation vote has been effectively delayed by two holdout senators, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, both Republicans, who say they will withhold their votes until they get written assurances from the DOJ concerning the payout fund and a deal shielding the president and his businesses from future IRS tax audits. But Trump’s own comments on Friday illustrate how differently the president views the $1.8 billion pool of money. He said the Jan. 6 rioters’ lives had been “unfairly and illegally destroyed” by former President Joe Biden’s administration, adding that “perhaps there has never been a group of people treated so badly in our nation’s history.” “I will always feel that these victims of government abuse should be paid back for what they were forced to endure, their lives have been ruined,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . He said Cornyn had agreed with him before losing to the president’s preferred Senate candidate in a runoff this spring. Tillis said the president’s post “is exactly why we are attempting to formally end” the fund, lamenting that Blanche’s confirmation has been held up “only because an incompetent personal advisor to the president refuses to amend the bogus settlement.” Tillis and Cornyn have been working toward an agreement with Blanche and the DOJ this week. However, Trump has said he is fine with waiting on the nomination until the two are out of office. Both senators lost their reelection bids to Trump-backed opponents, and have used their remaining Senate leverage to force action to kill the “anti-weaponization” fund and the IRS settlement’s audit immunity deal. “I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday as negotiations continued on the Hill. “Maybe they think I’m just going to give up or go along, but they’re mistaken,” Cornyn said on Wednesday after the DOJ canceled a joint meeting. Friday’s filing is a notice of appeal to the 11th Circuit that it will be challenging Williams’ ruling and contains no legal arguments.

title: Trump: I'm Fine Withdrawing Blanche Until Tillis and Cornyn Leave Office
author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
summary: Trump said the pair of senators were withholding their votes as an act of retaliation after the president refused to endorse them.
content: Alex Brandon/AP Photo/Alex Brandon President Donald Trump said he had “no objection” to temporarily withdrawing Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general until Republican Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina leave office. The pair, who lost bitterly contested primaries after Trump opted not to back them, have refused to vote for Blanche over concerns that he and the Justice Department have not done enough to kill a proposed $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund for Trump’s political allies and a deal shielding the president and his businesses from future tax audits. Trump claimed on Truth Social Thursday that Cornyn and Tillis were withholding their key votes as retaliation for their losses in primary elections earlier this year. “John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee, who will remain, in any event, as Acting,” Trump wrote. “I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office.” Cornyn suggested on social media after Trump’s post that there were additional lawmakers who also had similar concerns about Trump’s settlement with the IRS that was signed by Blanche. Cornyn’s post did not indicate whether any other concerned parties were also considering voting no on his confirmation. Cornyn told reporters on Thursday that Trump attributing the stalled vote to an act of revenge was a “convenient excuse, but it’s certainly not true.” The Texas Republican called off a meeting with Blanche on Wednesday, alleging that the Justice Department was not “responsive” to his requests. Cornyn said he sent the Justice Department line-by-line edits to its proposal on the audit exemption deal and the $1. billion “anti-weaponization” fund that would compensate individuals whom the federal government investigated under the Biden administration. The Senate Judiciary Committee delayed advancing a vote for Blanche’s confirmation on Wednesday evening, stating that Cornyn and Tillis wanted written assurance from the Justice Department. Tillis said Thursday he still saw a path forward in the negotiations, but that he did not “understand all of this drama.” “Everybody's saying that it's just a few details to sort out the audit. Well, why on Earth is the president now weighing in and saying no, unless somebody's told him that maybe you want to keep these vehicles in place because you could use them someday?” Tillis told reporters. “That is a horrible look. You can't explain it. … If I were running, there's no way I could excuse this or explain it.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R–South Dakota) said Thursday that the best strategy to confirm Blanche required resolving Cornyn’s and Tillis’ questions. “I'll defer to whatever the White House and president decide they want to do,” he said. Senator Dick Durbin (D–Illinois), the ranking member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, said Trump’s threat to pull Blanche’s nomination rather than change the settlement indicated the president was “trying up the pressure” against the duo so that they change their position. Durbin said he had “no doubt” that concerns about the settlement were more widespread in the Republican Party — but that others were “afraid to say the first word about it.” “These two senators, like me, are lame ducks, and they have more courage to deal with these issues than their colleagues,” Durbin said.

title: Senate Advances Trump’s CDC Picks, With Bill Cassidy Setting Aside Concerns
author: Margaret Manto
summary: Cassidy, the Republican chair of the Senate’s health committee, had previously voiced reservations about the picks' abilities to separate themselves from RFK Jr.’s views on vaccines.
content: Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana) ultimately said he would support Schwartz after the CDC updated a webpage about vaccines and autism to remove a reference to him. J. Scott Applewhite/AP Senate Republicans advanced Erica Schwartz’s nomination to lead the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, paving the way for the administration’s pick to be confirmed by the full Senate. Schwartz , a former chief medical officer of the Coast Guard, served as a deputy U.S. surgeon general during the first Trump administration. Her public health bona fides put her on slightly better footing with the Senate Committee for Health, Education, Labor and Pensions, though the committee’s chair, Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana), still pressed Schwartz on whether she would stand up to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. During her confirmation hearing, Schwartz told Cassidy that she would “never betray the science.” Cassidy, who lost his bid for a third term earlier this year, ultimately said he would support Schwartz after the CDC updated a webpage about vaccines and autism to remove a reference to him. The web page previously said that it contained the phrase “vaccines do not cause autism” only to appease Cassidy . Last week, that statement was removed, and replaced with: “Scientists have not identified the root causes of autism. HHS continues to support rigorous scientific research and will update this page as reliable new evidence becomes available.” Cassidy, who has been a critic of Kennedy’s vaccine policies, also supported the nomination of Sean Kaufman to serve as the assistant secretary for preparedness and response. The committee also voted to advance Kaufman’s nomination to the full Senate. Kaufman’s past comments questioning the safety and efficacy of vaccines drew the senator’s ire during his appearance before HELP. Cassidy said at the outset of Thursday’s vote that he had received assurances from HHS that Kaufman would not be involved in vaccine policy or be the ultimate decision-maker on issues like mRNA vaccines. “We can’t have perfection,” Cassidy said. He that the administration is “committed to continuing to work to remove misinformation” from the CDC web page on vaccines and autism, which remains online. He also said that “several actions have been taken” to address decisions relating to vaccines and autism at HHS, including “key personnel changes and better oversight.” The CDC has been without a permanent director since last August, when Susan Monarez was ousted for disagreeing with Kennedy on vaccine policy decisions. National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya has served as acting leader of the CDC since then.

title: Judiciary Committee Delays Blanche Nomination Vote
author: Al Weaver
summary: Sen. John Cornyn said the acting attorney general and the Department of Justice have “stonewalled” his demands.
content: The Texas Republican had hoped for a resolution ahead of the committee vote. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call via AP Images) The Senate Judiciary Committee has officially delayed a vote on Todd Blanche’s nomination to become attorney general, as he struggles to secure the support of two key Senate Republicans. Standing in the way of Blanche’s promotion from acting attorney general are Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina), with Cornyn saying that Blanche and the Justice Department haven’t done enough to ease his concerns over the proposed $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund and a deal shielding President Donald Trump from future tax audits. “[Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley] works to set President Trump’s nominees up for success in committee, not failure,” a spokesperson for the committee said. “Senators Cornyn and Tillis want written assurances from the Department of Justice regarding the Trump-IRS settlement. Tomorrow’s markup is postponed as work continues to secure sufficient support in committee to favorably report Attorney General-nominee Todd Blanche, who is highly qualified for the job.” A “no” vote by either Cornyn or Tillis would likely doom Blanche’s nomination. “They’ve stonewalled it,” Cornyn told reporters on Wednesday. “They’re making this a lot harder than it needs to be. … They claim to be negotiating in good faith, but something’s not working, and I don’t know where the problem is. We’re trying to make it easy on them. They simply refuse to take our help.” The Texas Republican had hoped for a resolution Wednesday morning as he was scheduled to meet with Blanche, but instead he canceled that meeting, alleging that DOJ was not “responsive” to his asks — particularly on the scope of the tax audit proposal. He also said that he sent the Justice Department line-by-line edits to their proposal on the “anti-weaponization” fund and the audit immunity deal. Later in the day, Cornyn huddled with Tillis and Grassley to brief them on the situation. Grassley delayed the vote hours later, with Cornyn continuing to wonder why Blanche’s team has not been sufficiently responsive. “I would think [Blanche] wants to be confirmed,” Cornyn said. “I don’t think he’s going to be confirmed if he doesn’t at least try to be responsive.” Cornyn has insisted Blanche put in writing that the anti-weaponization fund will not go forward, adding that Blanche’s word that it’s “ ” and “moot” is insufficient. Cornyn has noted repeatedly that the agreement between the IRS and the president could be revived later via a breach of contract lawsuit — meaning that a change must be made in writing. Amid the tumult, Blanche held meetings elsewhere on Capitol Hill, including with Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah), another holdout if Blanche’s nomination were to make it out of the Judiciary committee, and Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyoming). Cornyn, the former No. 2 Senate Republican, has long been an ally of leadership, but has been putting his new-found freedom to use after he lost his primary in May. He dispelled speculation on Wednesday that he will fall in line despite his ongoing skepticism of Blanche and the DOJ's deal with Trump. “Maybe they think they can roll me,” Cornyn told reporters, adding that’s not the case. Other Republicans on the committee think Cornyn will stick to his guns. “If I were the Justice Department, I would believe him,” said Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana). “He’s as serious as four heart attacks and a stroke — and an aneurysm.” The delay has major implications for Blanche, as it means his nomination process to become the full-time attorney general will spill beyond the August recess. Republican leaders had been hoping to get him over the finish line before they leave for the five-week break late next week.

title: Fed Maintains Interest Rates as Trump Escalates His Threats Against Iran
author: Jade Lozada
summary: The committee cited “elevated uncertainty that owes, in part, to the conflict in the Middle East.”
content: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is being pulled in opposite directions by high inflation numbers and a president who has made no secret that he wants to see rates slashed. Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday as Chair Kevin Warsh and Fed officials contend with volatile oil prices and persistent inflation since the pandemic. “Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace despite elevated uncertainty that owes, in part, to the conflict in the Middle East,” the Federal Open Market Committee said in a statement . The Fed has now cited the conflict in the Middle East for contributing to economic uncertainty in four consecutive decisions to keep interest rates where they are. That hasn’t stopped President Donald Trump — who told Fox News Wednesday morning that the U.S. would “beat the fucking shit out” of Iran — from insisting on lower rates. Trump accused board members of standing in the way of lower rates, in a gaggle with reporters Monday. “Kevin’s fantastic, but he’s got a board, and the board members are very political,” Trump said. “You need the consent of some people that have perhaps bad intentions.” The Fed’s rate-setting committee voted 9-3 to preserve rates at 3.5 to 3.75% for the fifth consecutive meeting since December, citing elevated inflation stemming in part from energy prices and strong productivity growth and capital investment. The three officials in the minority voted to raise rates by a quarter percentage point. Officials indicated in their quarterly projections last month — a practice that Warsh has criticized for revealing too much of the central bank’s thinking to eager investors — that rates may rise this year to tamp down inflation. Warsh is being pulled in opposite directions by high inflation numbers and a president who has made no secret that he wants to see rates slashed to stimulate economic growth. The annual inflation rate slowed from 4.2% in May to 3.5% in June as the U.S. and Iran settled into a ceasefire agreement, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The rate-setting committee maintains a goal of lowering inflation to 2%. The inflation rate last punched in at or below 2% in February . That goal increasingly appears far away for the central bank. Oil prices surged this month after Trump announced the end of the ceasefire with Iran on July 8. Warsh has his own qualms with Fed officials. The Fed chair wants to transform how the Fed communicates with the public. He has criticized officials’ “dot plot” economic projections and the practice of Fed governors delivering speeches on economic topics around the country. Warsh has also shortened interest rate announcements from the FOMC, saying markets are overly sensitive to Fed communications. Warsh recently appointed five task forces that will examine topics ranging from Fed communications to the impact of AI on the economy and the drivers of inflation. The members include university economists, former foreign central bankers and CEOs.

title: Blanche Committee Vote in Limbo After Cornyn Meeting Canceled
author: Al Weaver
summary: “Maybe they think I’m just going to give up or go along, but they’re mistaken,” Cornyn said.
content: A “no” vote by John Cornyn would likely doom Blanche’s chances of getting confirmed. (Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP) Sen. John Cornyn’s planned meeting on Wednesday with acting Attorney General Todd Blanche was canceled, imperiling the chances of his nomination advancing through the Judiciary Committee this week. The Texas Republican said he was "disappointed" to have to cancel the meeting due to the Department of Justice’s unwillingness to produce an ironclad change to the IRS settlement that spawned a proposed $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund and shielded President Donald Trump from future tax audits. The DOJ did not return a request for comment. The canceled meeting was slated to take place a day before the committee was scheduled to vote on Blanche’s nomination. Cornyn said that Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) wants an answer on how he will vote by 4 p.m. in case they need to postpone the markup. At this point, Cornyn remains an impediment. “I’m not prepared to vote ‘yes,’ let me put it that way,” Cornyn said when asked if he planned to vote “no” on Thursday. “Maybe they think I’m just going to give up or go along, but they’re mistaken,” Cornyn said of the DOJ’s lack of action on the fund. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina), another Judiciary Committee member, is aligned with Cornyn on what he needs to see from Blanche in order to support the nomination. “I think they realize now that we’re serious. I think [Sen. Thom Tillis] is pretty much on the same page that I am. They better get real. There’s not much time left,” Cornyn said. A “no” vote by either Cornyn or Tillis would likely doom Blanche’s chances of getting confirmed as attorney general. “We’ve still got another five to six hours. That’s plenty of time to resolve this,” Cornyn continued. “There’s no real need to have a meeting if they produce the documentation that we requested and that he testified to under oath in his hearing.” Cornyn has insisted that Blanche put in writing that the anti-weaponization fund will not go forward and that Blanche’s word that it is “ ” is insufficient. The Texas senator has noted repeatedly that the deal could be revived later via a breach of contract lawsuit, meaning that a change must be made in writing. “I haven’t seen a single piece of writing that is responsive to what I requested. … There’s been a lot of back and forth with my staff. I don’t know if it’s been the reluctance of the DOJ staff," he said. Republicans have been hoping to confirm Blanche next week before they depart for the Senate’s annual August recess.

title: Fauci Repeatedly Invokes the Fifth at Rand Paul’s COVID Hearing
author: Margaret Manto
summary: In his opening statement, Fauci told the committee that he believed Paul had an “unhinged obsession” with jailing him.
content: Allison Robbert/AP Photo/Allison Robbert Former infectious disease official Anthony Fauci refused to answer questions in a contentious Wednesday morning hearing held by his outspoken critic, Republican Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, repeatedly invoking the Fifth Amendment. In his opening statement, Fauci told the Senate Committee on Homeland Security & Governmental Affairs that he believed Paul had an “unhinged obsession” with jailing him, and the only reason he was holding the hearing was to try to catch Fauci in a lie. “Therefore, although it pains me to do so because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress, under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions,” Fauci said. Despite the witness’s lack of cooperation, Paul proceeded with questioning Fauci. The senator has long pushed theories that the COVID-19 virus emerged from a lab in China, and that Fauci was aware of this — and knowingly funding risky infectious disease work at the Chinese lab in question. Most scientists agree that the pandemic originated from a natural source, probably a wild animal. As promised, Fauci refused to answer any questions. “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment to the Constitution,” he said repeatedly in his light Brooklyn drawl. At one point, Fauci’s lawyer, David Schertler, attempted to address the committee. Paul had security remove him from the hearing room. Many members of the audience applauded his removal as he left. In a written statement provided to NOTUS, Schertler said that the circumstances surrounding the hearing, including Paul’s repeated calls for Fauci’s imprisonment and the “foreseeable result of these outlandish statements” — including harassment and death threats towards Fauci and members of his family — “regrettably made his continued cooperation impossible.” “The accusations that Chairman Paul continues to propagate are false and disgraceful, and we will examine all options to hold him accountable,” Schertler said in the statement. Paul told Fauci the committee would have to consider “what appropriate action” to take after the hearing in response to his refusal to answer questions. “There will be repercussions to your refusal to testify today,” Paul told Fauci. “It’s against the law to obstruct an investigation of Congress.” Courts have previously upheld a witness’s right to invoke the Fifth Amendment in response to a congressional subpoena if they fear self-incrimination. In recent history, the former CEO of ActBlue and a former Biden aide have also declined to answer questions in hearings. Paul and others who opposed the federal government’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic have repeatedly called for Fauci’s imprisonment. In response, former President Joe Biden issued Fauci a preemptive pardon before leaving office. Paul’s frustration with Fauci was apparent even before the former health official revealed his strategy. “Frankly, the American people deserve an apology,” Paul told Fauci in his opening statement as chair of the committee. “That loss of trust may be your most damaging legacy,” Paul said, speaking from a teleprompter. Fauci led the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases from until and played a key role in the global fight against AIDS as well as COVID-19. The hearing took place in one of the smaller Senate hearing rooms. Many of the seats were reserved for guests of Paul’s committee. Included in the audience was Mary Holland, CEO of Children’s Health Defense, a vaccine-skeptical organization formerly led by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. “Ladies and gentlemen, I’m going to have to ask you to put two masks on,” a man sitting in a committee-reserved seat said jokingly to his neighbors before the hearing began. It’s the culmination of a frenetic week for both Paul and Fauci. On Tuesday, Paul published excerpts from Fauci’s diary from the pandemic years, claiming that he orchestrated a cover-up of the fact that the pandemic originated in a lab and was the result of so-called “gain-of-function” research, or laboratory work on infectious diseases that makes them more dangerous to humans. Soon after the release of the diary excerpts, the Trump administration released new guidance prohibiting federal funding going to what it deems gain-of-function research. Scientists have raised concerns that overly broad restrictions could disrupt important research into infectious diseases. Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wisconsin), another Fauci critic, attempted to question Fauci on whether the pulmonary infarction he wrote about in the released diary could have been caused by the COVID-19 vaccine. Johnson has repeatedly claimed that the federal government suppressed evidence of dangerous side effects caused by the vaccine. In contrast to Paul’s threats of repercussions, one Republican appeared to affirm Fauci’s right to decline to answer questions. Like Paul, Sen. James Lankford (R-Oklahoma) attempted to question Fauci on whether the virus originated from a lab. But Lankford responded, “as is your right to do,” when Fauci invoked his right to not answer the question. Democrats on the committee apologized to Fauci for his being compelled to appear. “We are here in an attempt to entrap you,” Sen. Margaret Wood Hassan (D-New Hampshire) said during her questioning period, in which she did not actually ask Fauci any questions. Gary Peters (D-Michigan), the ranking member of the committee, accused Paul of ignoring the actual duties of the committee in favor of promoting his theories around COVID-19. He pointed to cuts to the public health agencies as the more pressing issue at hand. “Instead of focusing on the national security challenges that we are facing in our country right now, today’s hearing looks backwards, revisiting questions this committee has already examined,” Peters said. “History tells us, unfortunately, another pandemic is all but inevitable. The question is whether Congress and this committee will work to better prepare our country for it, or continue looking backward while our public health infrastructure crumbles around us.”

title: Cornyn to Meet With Blanche Ahead of Critical Confirmation Vote
author: Torrie Herrington
summary: The Texas senator is a key holdout leading up to the Judiciary Committee vote to advance Blanche’s nomination Thursday
content: Texas Sen. John Cornyn is a key swing vote on the Senate Judiciary Committee, split 12-10 between Republicans and Democrats. An even break would effectively kill the nomination. Allison Robbert/AP Photo Sen. John Cornyn said he will meet with acting Attorney General Todd Blanche on Wednesday about killing President Donald Trump’s controversial settlement fund — a requirement for the Texas Republican to vote for his confirmation this week. “I told him we need paper. We need it in writing. We don't need well wishes or, you know, impressions,” the Texas Republican told reporters Tuesday afternoon. “We need concrete confirmation of what he testified to in his hearing." Cornyn is a key swing vote on the Senate Judiciary Committee, split 12-10 between Republicans and Democrats. An even break would effectively kill the nomination. “Fake news alert: there is no ‘deal’ on Blanche nom. They know what they have to do.” Cornyn posted on X earlier in the day. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) — who also lost his reelection bid and will leave Congress next year — has also made it clear that he’s not an automatic “yes” on Blanche. “The key for Todd, or anybody going through Judiciary Committee, is being pretty tight on January the 6th. They better not have said for one minute that the people that beat up police officers … were righteous people,” Tillis said in June. “You come even close to saying that, you don’t have a [chance] of getting my vote in Judiciary.” Blanche has repeatedly told senators that the proposed $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund, part of Trump’s settlement with the IRS, is and won’t be coming back. But Cornyn has pointed out that Blanche has acknowledged that the proposed "anti-weaponization" fund remains on paper as part of the settlement with Trump. "What I want is the written document to say the same thing he did in his sworn testimony in front of the Judiciary Committee, and, as you recall, what he said is the weaponization fund is . He said the audit immunity basically doesn't extend to parties beyond the lawsuit, and it doesn't also extend to future actions by federal agencies other than the IRS," Cornyn told reporters Monday.

title: Senate Confirms Jay Clayton as Director of National Intelligence
author: Avani Kalra
summary: He will replace acting director Bill Pulte and his confirmation could unlock Democratic votes to renew a crucial spy powers tool.
content: The Senate confirmed Jay Clayton as director of national intelligence along party lines, even as Democrats say he’ll be an improvement over the acting head, Bill Pulte. Tom Williams/AP The Senate voted on Tuesday to confirm Jay Clayton as the next head of the Office of the Director of National Intelligence 51-47, with no Democrats voting to support his nomination. Clayton is currently the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York and was previously the chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission. He will take over the role from Acting DNI Director Bill Pulte, who has been criticized by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle for his lack of intelligence experience.
